Following one curve tells us what happened as LLaMA trained longer, not how the two families compare. ### What the experiments show GPT-1's authors checked the value of pretraining by fine-tuning a Transformer on the same tasks starting from random weights. In [Table 5, §5](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf#page=8), the mean score across eight tasks is 74.7 with pretraining and 59.9 without it. The 14.8-point difference measures the value of transferring weights before fine-tuning, not the effect of changing a prompt. LAMBADA asks the model to predict the last word of a passage. The weights can stay fixed while we change the prompt or the rule for choosing the word. GPT-2 scored 52.66% without filtering and 63.24% with a stop-word filter ([§3.3](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf#page=5)). GPT-3 175B scored 76.2% with plain continuation and 86.4% with 15 demonstrations. In the latter setting the authors also changed the format, from completing a passage to filling in a blank. One demonstration in the new format scored 72.5%, below plain continuation. The gap between 86.4% and 76.2% therefore includes the effect of changing the format ([GPT-3, §3.1.2, Table 3.2 and Figure 3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2005.14165v4#S3.SS1.SSS2)). [LLaMA, Table 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.13971v1#S2.T3) compares GPT-3 175B and LLaMA 13B without demonstrations. On HellaSwag, where the model chooses a plausible continuation, GPT-3 gets 78.9% and LLaMA gets 79.2%. On PIQA, where it chooses a solution to an everyday physical problem, the order reverses: 81.0% and 80.1%. These are reported results, not an experiment that varies only model size. The 0.3-point HellaSwag gap does not isolate the effect of RoPE. The models differ in size by about 13.5 times. The rough pretraining compute estimate $6ND$ accounts for both the number of weights $N$ and the number of tokens processed $D$. For GPT-3 175B and 300 billion tokens, that gives about $3.15\cdot10^{23}$ FLOP. For LLaMA 13B and one trillion tokens, it gives $7.8\cdot10^{22}$ FLOP. The gap is about fourfold rather than 13.5-fold because the smaller model processed more tokens. These estimates do not measure GPU time.
